title: Using Node.js
summary: Checks the installed Node version from the VS Code terminal, introduces the Node REPL (enter, try JS, exit), and then runs a whole JavaScript file with the node command from the correct folder.

concepts.heading: Version check in the VS Code terminal
points: Open a new VS Code window, then View > Terminal (or drag the panel up from the bottom edge of the window).
node -v (same as node --version) prints the installed version, starting with a 'v'. The course needs version 18 or later.
If your number differs: a higher one is fine (newer release); a lower one usually means an older install is still on the machine. The previous install lesson's notes/FAQ explain the fix.

concepts.heading: The Node REPL
points: REPL = Read, Eval, Print, Loop: an interactive prompt that reads a line of code, evaluates it, prints the result, then waits for the next line. Most languages have one; it is not Node-specific.
Start it by typing node on its own. A welcome message and a > prompt show you are inside.
.exit leaves the REPL (the > prompt disappears). Pressing Ctrl+C twice also exits.
Ctrl+C is the general escape hatch for the command line: if a process is running and you have lost your normal prompt, press it once or twice.
Any JavaScript works because Node is a JavaScript runtime: 5 + 8 prints 13; let a = 3 then a + 12 prints 15.
It behaves like the browser's DevTools console, but runs outside the browser.

concepts.heading: Running a JavaScript file with Node
points: The REPL is handy for quick tests, but real apps are written in files that Node executes.
Starting files: download the lesson zip '2.1 Using Node' from the lecture resources, extract it and open the folder in VS Code. It holds an empty index.js.
Write code in index.js and save it.
In the terminal, cd into the folder that contains the file. Dragging the folder into the terminal after typing cd fills in its path.
Run node followed by the file name: node index.js. Node loads the file, executes it top to bottom, and console.log output appears in the terminal.

Tab completion: type the first letters of a file name and press Tab to auto-complete it. If nothing completes, the file isn't in the current directory, which is a quick check that you are in the right folder.

# v20.11.0  (any version >= 18)

task.name: 2.1 Using Node: run your first file
task.starting_point: Extracted '2.1 Using Node' folder opened in VS Code, containing a blank index.js.
task.goal: Execute a JavaScript file with the Node runtime from the terminal and see its output.
steps: Add console.log("Hello from Node"); to index.js and save.
cd into the '2.1 Using Node' folder (type cd, then drag the folder in, press Enter).
Type node ind and press Tab so it completes to node index.js; press Enter.
Extra practice suggested: create a second .js file in the same folder, write some code and run it with node <filename>.
task.expected_result: The terminal prints Hello from Node and returns to the normal prompt.

pitfalls: Running node index.js from the wrong directory gives a 'Cannot find module' error; Tab not completing the name is the early warning.
Getting stuck in the REPL: use .exit or Ctrl+C twice.
Typing node with no file name opens the REPL instead of running your file.
An old Node version (<18) left over from a previous install.

gaps_and_ideas: New lesson 's23-using-node' (blurb: use Node from the terminal, both interactively in the REPL and to run whole files). Note the reference repo names the file script.js; the course uses index.js.
Task 1: 'REPL simulator': a fake terminal where the learner types node, evaluates 3 expressions (5 + 8, let a = 3, a + 12) and exits with .exit; check each prompt/response.
Task 2: given a fake file tree and a current-directory indicator, choose the right cd command so that node index.js succeeds.
Task 3: write index.js that logs two lines; the sandbox shows the terminal output as it would appear after node index.js.
Explore demo: a terminal mock with Tab completion that only completes names present in the current folder, so learners see why Tab failing means the wrong directory.
